title: The Follow-Through Mistake Teachers Keep Making
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a subtle error that undermines even teachers who consistently enforce their classroom management plan: adding personal commentary such as lecturing, questioning, glaring, sighing, or reprimanding on top of a stated consequence. He explains this is a mistake for three specific reasons -- it breaks the teacher's word by exceeding the consequence students were promised, it creates simmering resentment that students often act on through later revenge rather than open confrontation, and it blocks the internal reflection that consequences are actually designed to produce. His central argument is that real behavior change requires students to wrestle privately with their own conscience, which can only happen once the teacher is emotionally out of the picture. The concrete technique is to deliver the stated consequence like a neutral referee and then physically and verbally disengage, letting the classroom management plan do the work without any added editorializing.
points: Adding a lecture, glare, or sigh on top of a stated consequence breaks the implicit promise a teacher made when the plan was first taught.
Students rarely confront a teacher who 'adds to' a consequence; instead they let it simmer as resentment and seek revenge later.
Real reflection only happens once the teacher is emotionally out of the picture, since resentment blocks the internal accountability process.
The fix is to deliver consequences like a referee -- calm, clear, and emotionally unaffected -- then get out of the way entirely.
quotes: However, despite your consistency, if you make this one mistake during your follow-through, you’ll undermine the most important factor in curbing misbehavior.
The mistake is this: Instead of simply informing the misbehaving student of their consequence, you give your own two cents. In other words, you add to the consequence.
If someone in your friendship circle goes back on their word, you’d be angry. Of course. Your students are no different. Only, they keep it close to the vest.
They must wrestle with their conscience, consider how their misbehavior affects others, and conclude that being a valuable member of the class is more desirable than misbehaving.
Internal struggle, which is essential for real behavior change, only happens when you’re out of the picture. Your job is to follow-through like a referee—calm, clear, and emotionally unaffected.
